issues.legal_issue: Entries in official records concerning a person's age or birth are not conclusive merely because they are admissible, and their probative value depends on proof of their authenticity and source.
material_facts: The dispute concerned whether the claimants were children entitled to inherit the recorded holder's land.
The challengers relied on electoral rolls, school records and other official documents to dispute the ages of the mother and children.
The ages recorded in those documents conflicted with one another and, if accepted together, produced impossible or absurd results.
The documents' sources of information and authenticity were not established by reliable supporting evidence.
issues.conclusion: The documents could be admissible, including under Section 35 of the Evidence Act, but their contradictions and lack of reliable proof meant they did not disprove the claimants' relationship or warrant rejecting their claim.
issues.legal_principle: Admissibility and probative value are distinct. Under Section 35 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, an official entry may be admissible, but the court must assess its source, authenticity, proof and need for corroboration; the ordinary civil or criminal standard of proof applies. The court relied on State of Bihar v. Radha Krishna Singh, AIR 1983 SC 684; Ram Prasad Sharma v. State of Bihar, AIR 1970 SC 326; Ram Murti v. State of Haryana, AIR 1970 SC 1029; Dayaram v. Dawalatshah, AIR 1971 SC 681; Harpal Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh, AIR 1981 SC 361; Ravinder Singh Gorkhi v. State of U.P., (2006) 5 SCC 584; Babloo Pasi v. State of Jharkhand, (2008) 13 SCC 133; Desh Raj v. Bodh Raj, AIR 2008 SC 632; Ram Suresh Singh v. Prabhat Singh, (2009) 6 SCC 681; Mohd. Ikram Hussain v. State of U.P., AIR 1964 SC 1625; Santenu Mitra v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1999 SC 1587; and, concerning proof of dates of birth, Sections 32(5), 50, 51, 59, 60 and 61 of the Evidence Act and Updesh Kumar v. Prithvi Singh, (2001) 2 SCC 524, and State of Punjab v. Mohinder Singh, AIR 2005 SC 1868.

rule.if: age_or_birth_dispute and official_record_entries_relied_on and (contradictory_entries or source_and_authenticity_unproved)

predicates.age_or_birth_dispute: The proceeding involved a dispute about a person's age or date of birth.
predicates.official_record_entries_relied_on: A party relied on entries in official records to establish a person's age or date of birth.
predicates.contradictory_entries: The relied-on records contained entries that conflicted with one another or led to impossible or absurd results.
predicates.source_and_authenticity_unproved: The party relying on the entries did not reliably establish their source and authenticity.

issues.definition: When a party relies on official entries in an age or birth dispute and the entries are contradictory or their source and authenticity are unproved, those entries are not conclusive without reliable proof.

issues.legal_issue: Long-term cohabitation as spouses gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of marriage, and children born of that relationship are not presumed illegitimate.
material_facts: The recorded landholder and the children's mother lived together as husband and wife for a long period after his first wife's death.
Their relationship was accepted as a marital relationship by family members and the community.
The claimants and other children were born from the relationship.
The challengers relied on contradictory age documents, but did not produce unimpeachable evidence rebutting the relationship or the presumption arising from it.
issues.conclusion: The long-standing relationship gave rise to a presumption of marriage, and the children could not be treated as illegitimate on the material relied on by the challengers; their claim to be recorded as heirs was not disproved.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, cohabitation under the same roof for a number of years permits a presumption that the couple lived as husband and wife and that their children are not illegitimate. The law favours marriage over concubinage where a man and woman have cohabited continuously for years, although the presumption may be rebutted by unimpeachable evidence. The court relied on S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v. Suruttayan, AIR 1992 SC 756 and (1994) 1 SCC 460; Mohabbat Ali Khan v. Mohd. Ibrahim Khan, AIR 1929 PC 135; Gokalchand v. Parvin Kumar, AIR 1952 SC 231; Ranganath Parmeshwar Panditrao Mali v. Eknath Gajanan Kulkarni, (1996) 7 SCC 681; and Sobha Hymavathi Devi v. Setti Gangadhara Swamy, (2005) 2 SCC 244. It also referred to S. Khushboo v. Kanniammal, (2010) 5 SCC 600, relying on Lata Singh v. State of U.P., AIR 2006 SC 2522, concerning live-in relationships between unmarried adults of different sexes.

rule.if: inheritance_or_status_dispute and long_term_cohabitation_as_spouses and relationship_accepted_by_family_or_community and children_born_of_relationship and not unimpeachable_rebuttal_evidence

predicates.inheritance_or_status_dispute: The proceeding concerned a claim to inherit property or establish family status.
predicates.long_term_cohabitation_as_spouses: A man and woman lived together for a long period in a relationship as spouses.
predicates.relationship_accepted_by_family_or_commu: The relationship was accepted as marital by family members or the community.
predicates.children_born_of_relationship: Children were born from the couple's relationship.
predicates.unimpeachable_rebuttal_evidence: The opposing party produced unimpeachable evidence rebutting the presumption of marriage or the children's status.

issues.definition: In an inheritance or status dispute, long-term cohabitation as spouses, social or family acceptance, and children born of the relationship give rise to a presumption of marriage and legitimacy unless unimpeachable evidence rebuts it.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent factual findings in a statutory land-rights proceeding should not be disturbed in a further appeal when the material relied on to show perversity is unreliable or contradictory.
material_facts: Three statutory authorities considered the evidence and found that the claimants were children of the recorded landholder and entitled to have their names recorded as heirs.
The High Court declined to interfere with those concurrent findings in judicial review.
The challengers asked the Supreme Court to reassess the evidence on the ground that the findings were perverse.
The principal documents relied on by the challengers contradicted one another and, taken together, produced impossible or absurd results.
The Supreme Court found no special circumstances in that material warranting further reassessment or interference.
issues.conclusion: The concurrent findings were left undisturbed, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory authorities under the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, exercise powers of civil and revenue courts and may decide questions of title and inheritance; Section 48 provides for revision. Where three such authorities have made concurrent factual findings after considering the evidence, a further appeal does not warrant reassessment merely because a party alleges perversity. The court must have material that justifies interference; unreliable or contradictory documents that do not displace the findings are insufficient.

predicates.appeal_challenging_concurrent_statutory_: The proceeding was an appeal challenging concurrent factual findings made by statutory authorities in a land-rights or inheritance matter.
predicates.findings_based_on_assessed_evidence: The statutory authorities reached their findings after considering the evidence presented by the parties.
predicates.alleged_perversity_supported_only_by_unr: The party alleging perversity relied only on material that was unreliable or contradictory and did not displace the factual findings.

issues.definition: In an appeal challenging concurrent statutory findings based on assessed evidence, unreliable or contradictory material alone does not justify disturbing those findings.
